description: The French R is produced in the back of the throat (uvular). It sounds like a gentle gargle, NOT like an English R or a Spanish rolled R. It's one of the most distinctive French sounds.
how_to_produce: Open your mouth slightly
Keep your tongue tip DOWN behind your lower teeth
Raise the back of your tongue toward your soft palate (the back roof of your mouth)
Push air through the narrow gap — it should vibrate gently
Think of it like a very soft gargle or the 'ch' in Scottish 'loch' but voiced
common_mistakes: Using an English R (tongue tip curled up) — keep tongue tip DOWN
Rolling the R like Spanish — this is a completely different sound
Making it too harsh or guttural — it should be soft and smooth
Dropping the R entirely — it should always be audible

practice_pairs.explanation: R vs L — feel the difference: R is in the throat, L is with the tongue tip
king vs law — same contrast, R (throat) vs L (tongue)

description: French has four nasal vowels — vowel sounds where air flows through both the mouth AND the nose. They're the sounds that make French sound distinctly French. English doesn't have true nasal vowels.
how_to_produce: Start with a regular vowel sound (ah, eh, oh)
Lower your soft palate to let air flow through your nose at the same time
DO NOT touch your tongue to the roof of your mouth — the N/M is NOT pronounced as a consonant
Think of it as the vowel 'humming' through your nose
Test: pinch your nose — if the sound changes, you're nasalizing correctly
common_mistakes: Pronouncing the N or M as a full consonant — 'bon' is NOT 'bonn', it's a nasalized 'boh'
Not nasalizing at all — just saying 'bo' without the nasal quality
Confusing the different nasal vowels — each has a distinct mouth shape

practice_pairs.explanation: bon (nasal, no N sound) vs bonne (N is pronounced) — masculine vs feminine
vin (nasal ɛ̃) vs vaine (eh + n sound) — different meanings entirely

description: French 'u' (written u) and 'ou' (written ou) are two different vowels that English speakers often confuse. French U is made with lips rounded AND tongue pushed forward. OU is like English 'oo'. Mixing them up changes word meanings.
how_to_produce: For French U (y): Say 'ee' as in 'see', then round your lips WITHOUT moving your tongue
Your tongue should be at the front of your mouth, lips tightly rounded
For OU (u): This is the easy one — say 'oo' as in 'food'
The key difference: tongue FRONT for U, tongue BACK for OU
common_mistakes: Saying 'oo' for both — this makes 'rue' (street) sound like 'roue' (wheel)
Not rounding the lips enough for U
Moving the tongue back when trying to say U — keep it forward

practice_pairs.explanation: street vs wheel — French U vs OU. Listen for the tongue position difference
above vs below — U (front tongue) vs OU (back tongue)

description: French words are full of letters that aren't pronounced, especially at the end. Most final consonants (S, T, D, X, Z, P) are silent. This is one of the biggest adjustments for English speakers.
how_to_produce: General rule: final consonants are silent (petit, grand, vous, beaucoup)
Exceptions: C, R, F, L are usually pronounced at the end (CaReFuL mnemonic)
Silent E at the end: 'table', 'chose' — the E just opens the preceding consonant
Double letters often simplify: 'appelle' has two P's but they sound like one
common_mistakes: Pronouncing every letter — 'petit' is 'puh-TEE' not 'puh-TEET'
Always dropping final R — 'bonjour' DOES end with R (it's in the CaReFuL exception list)
Ignoring liaison — sometimes those silent finals DO come alive before vowels

practice_pairs.explanation: The T is silent in 'petit' (masculine) but pronounced in 'petite' (feminine)
The D is silent in 'grand' but pronounced in 'grande'

description: Liaison is when a normally silent final consonant is pronounced because the next word starts with a vowel. It creates smooth, connected speech and is essential to sounding natural in French.
how_to_produce: When a word ending in a silent consonant is followed by a word starting with a vowel, pronounce that consonant
S and X become Z in liaison: 'les‿amis' → 'lez-ah-MEE'
D becomes T: 'grand‿ami' → 'grahn-tah-MEE'
N stays N: 'bon‿appétit' → 'boh-nah-pay-TEE'
Flow the linked consonant into the next word smoothly — no pause
common_mistakes: Pausing between words instead of flowing — liaison should be seamless
Making liaison where it shouldn't happen (e.g., after 'et' — never liaison after 'et')
Keeping the original consonant sound — remember S→Z, D→T in liaison

practice_pairs.explanation: Liaison happens before vowel (amis) but NOT before consonant (garçons)
N links to vowel in 'un ami' but stays silent before 'garçon'

description: French has two distinct E sounds: É (closed, like 'ay') and È (open, like 'eh'). The accent marks tell you which one to use. Getting them right improves comprehension and makes you sound more natural.
how_to_produce: É (closed E): Smile slightly, tongue high and forward. Say 'ay' as in 'say' but shorter
È (open E): Open mouth more, tongue lower. Say 'eh' as in 'bed'
É often appears at word endings (-é, -er, -ez): parlé, parler, parlez
È often appears in closed syllables or with grave accent: père, mère, crème
common_mistakes: Using the same E sound for both — French speakers DO hear the difference
Confusing the accent marks: é (closed, 'ay') vs è (open, 'eh')
Over-pronouncing É as a diphthong 'ay-ee' — keep it short and pure

practice_pairs.explanation: summer (closed É) vs was (open È) — listen for mouth openness
the (closed E) vs milk (open E) — subtle but meaningful

description: French H is always silent — never pronounced. But there are two types: H muet (mute H, allows liaison and elision) and H aspiré (aspirated H, blocks liaison and elision). You must memorize which words have which type.
how_to_produce: H muet (most H words): Treat as if the H isn't there — l'hôtel, l'homme, l'heure
H aspiré (some H words): Keep the article separate — le haricot, la honte, le héros
Neither type is actually pronounced — the difference is about what happens to the words BEFORE them
H aspiré words are marked in dictionaries with an asterisk or other symbol
common_mistakes: Actually pronouncing the H — French H is ALWAYS silent
Eliding before H aspiré — saying 'l'haricot' instead of 'le haricot'
Not eliding before H muet — saying 'le hôtel' instead of 'l'hôtel'

practice_pairs.explanation: H muet (elision: l'hôtel) vs H aspiré (no elision: le héros)

description: French has two nasal vowels that English speakers often confuse: EN/AN (ɑ̃, like a nasalized 'ah') and IN/AIN (ɛ̃, like a nasalized 'eh'). They appear in many common words and mixing them up can cause confusion.
how_to_produce: EN/AN (ɑ̃): Open mouth wide, say 'ah' through your nose — enfant, dans, encore
IN/AIN (ɛ̃): Spread lips slightly, say 'eh' through your nose — vin, pain, bien
The mouth shape is the key difference: wide open (ɑ̃) vs slightly spread (ɛ̃)
Both spellings EN/AN make the same sound (ɑ̃). Both IN/AIN/EIN make the same sound (ɛ̃)
common_mistakes: Using the same nasal for both — they ARE different sounds
Not opening the mouth enough for EN/AN — it needs a wider opening
Pronouncing the N — remember these are nasal vowels, not vowel+N

practice_pairs.explanation: wind (ɑ̃) vs wine (ɛ̃) — open mouth for vent, spread for vin
slow (ɑ̃) vs linen (ɛ̃) — same contrast, different words
